title: the departure
hook: a king runs after a chariot, and a prince asks the driver to pretend he didn't hear

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure, part two. Bark clothes, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Did you call somewhere home for a minute? A new week begins, and today the chariot moves. Day five hundred thirty-three.

Anyone who has driven away from a parent standing in the driveway knows the problem. If you keep looking back, you can't leave. If you don't look back, it feels cruel. The charioteer Sumantra has the horses ready. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb in, with their weapons, a spade, a basket, and Sita's clothes for fourteen years. And as the chariot starts to roll, the whole city starts to run after it.
screen: `LOOKING BACK FROM THE DRIVEWAY.` → `THE CHARIOT STARTS TO ROLL.` → `THE CITY RUNS AFTER IT.`

segments.voice: Valmiki fills the streets with noise. People run beside the wheels. Some call to Sumantra to slow down so they can see Rama's face a little longer. And from the palace comes the old king himself, on foot, with Kausalya, crying out: wait, Sumantra, wait. Rama hears his father. He can't bear it, and he can't stop. So he says to the driver, quietly: go on. If the king asks later, tell him you didn't hear. Being told to stop and being told to go, Rama says, is pain either way. Better to make it short. The chariot pulls away. Dasharatha falls in the dust. His counselors lift him and tell him something old and gentle: when you hope for someone to come back, you shouldn't follow them too far. The king stands and watches until even the dust from the wheels is gone. But the people keep following. Old brahmins, too slow to keep up, call after the chariot. Rama, out of respect, gets down and walks, and Sita and Lakshmana walk with him. By evening, they reach the bank of the Tamasa river, and the whole crowd sleeps there around them. That night Rama lies awake. These people will follow us into the forest, he thinks, and lose their homes. So, before dawn, he wakes Sumantra. They harness the horses quietly, cross the river, and the driver turns the chariot a little way back toward the city before turning again, so that the tracks will confuse anyone following. When the people wake, Rama is gone. They search for the tracks, can't follow them, and walk home weeping.
screen: `THE CITY RUNS BESIDE THE WHEELS.` · `TELL HIM YOU DIDN'T HEAR.` · `DON'T FOLLOW TOO FAR.` · `A NIGHT BY THE TAMASA.` · then, large: `RAMA SLIPS AWAY BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone you had to leave, or who had to leave you: a move, a graduation, a hospital door, a last visit. Let the scene come back gently. Breathe in, and feel the pull to look back. Breathe out, and feel the need to go on. Neither is wrong. Let the breath hold both, the way Rama did on that road. If it helps, picture the dust settling. The bell holds the time.
The departure, part three: the road. The king runs after the chariot, the people follow to the Tamasa, and Rama slips away before dawn to spare them.
Your line: the departure. Today, when a goodbye is hard, make it kind and make it short. Day five hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Many Ramayana recitations slow down at the departure from Ayodhya; listeners often know by heart the image of the old king following the chariot until only its dust is left.

myth: Rama stops the chariot when his father calls
he tells Sumantra to go on, and to say he didn't hear.
the people of Ayodhya follow Rama to the Tamasa river
and the crowd sleeps on the bank around him.
Rama leaves the crowd behind while they sleep
before dawn, and the chariot doubles back to confuse the tracks.

fork.setup: you're Rama, by the Tamasa at night. the whole city has followed you and will lose their homes if they keep going. what do you do?
options: wake them and order them home.
let them come into the forest.
leave quietly before dawn and hide the tracks.
fork.reveal: he leaves before dawn, and Sumantra turns the chariot back and forth so the tracks can't be followed.

original.note: Sanskrit tamasā: the river where Rama spends his first night of exile; its name recalls tamas, darkness.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama simply rode out of Ayodhya.
what it means: the city followed him, and he slipped away before dawn to send them home.

what a scholar hears: the Tamasa is also the river where, in the Bala Kanda, Valmiki was bathing when he saw the birds and the first shloka was born, so the exile's first night falls on the poet's own river.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 40 (the chariot leaves; the king follows; 'tell him you didn't hear')
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 45–46 (the citizens follow; the night by the Tamasa; Rama leaves before dawn)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 2 (Valmiki at the Tamasa)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Rama's instruction to Sumantra ('say you didn't hear') and the reasoning: paraphrased; confirm.
The counselors' advice (one who wants someone back shouldn't follow far): confirm wording.
The note that tamasā recalls tamas is a gloss, not a claimed etymology; confirm or remove.
